iterations.narrative:
The metabolomics data reveal a strong perturbation of **galactose metabolic and galactosemia pathways** (KEGG map00052 / SMP00043 and SMP00182; FDR = 0.0, fold-enrichment ≈ 951). Six input metabolites—D-galactose (C00221), galactitol (C01697), galactinol (C01235), sucrose (C00089), myo-inositol (C00137), and glycerol (C00116)—anchor this cluster.

The most mechanistically informative driver is **galactitol**, the sugar alcohol that accumulates in classic galactosemia when galactose cannot be further metabolized via the Leloir pathway. Pathway-membership queries confirm galactitol is annotated in both the Galactose Metabolism (map00052) and Galactosemia (SMP00182) entries. **Galactinol**, the galactosyl-donor upstream of galactitol, and **myo-inositol**, a downstream product of inositol metabolism that intersects galactose chemistry, are likewise confirmed members of the same pathway entries.

A KEGG graph traversal confirms a reachable (bidirectional) path from **D-glucose (C00221)** to **galactitol (C01697)** in five steps via glyceraldehyde (C00267) and other Leloir intermediates, suggesting glucose serves as the upstream precursor driving galactitol accumulation under conditions of pathway bottleneck.

A secondary but significant signal appears in the **glycerophospholipid biosynthetic pathway** (Wikipathways WP2533; FDR = 7.9 × 10⁻⁵). Here, the driver compounds are **ethanolamine (C00189)**, **myo-inositol (C00137)**, and **glycerol (C00116)**, all confirmed members. Ethanolamine is annotated in phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis (SMP14212) and links glycerol to phospholipid head-group generation; KEGG graph analysis, however, found no direct path from ethanolamine to myo-inositol within six hops, suggesting these metabolites may co-regulate glycerophospholipid metabolism through parallel, rather than sequential, reactions.

**Biological significance.** The convergence on galactose metabolism points to impaired galactose catabolism or a surge in galactose flux in the treatment state, consistent with inborn metabolic stress, toxin exposure, or disrupted肠道 microbiota–derived galactose processing. Elevated galactitol is a known osmolite and can promote lens cataractogenesis and neuronal stress if chronic. The concurrent perturbation of glycerophospholipid metabolism implicates membrane-remodeling stress and possibly choline/ethanolamine cycle dysregulation, which affects cell-membrane integrity, signaling lipid production, and neurotransmission—relevant to the observed dopamine (C03758) alteration as well. This multi-pathway pattern suggests a systemic metabolic reconfiguration rather than a single-enzyme defect.
